body:
Reply with plain text only: no JSON, no code fences, no commentary before or after. Do not send messages to anyone else.

You are drafting dialogue for a Halloween D&D video game, "The Crooked Moon" (an original story; use only the names given here and invent no new people, places, monsters or history). The player leads a party of four adventurers; never name, describe or gender them, and never describe their faces. Setting: Wickermoor Hollow, a valley in an autumn that never ends.

SCENE: the morning after. The party has been shut in Druskenvald Estate, a haunted manor, through a night of horrors, and has destroyed the hag in its attic. The storm is gone and the night is still; the manor has settled into a gentler, still-odd shape. The Lord and Lady of the manor (Phillip and Adela Druskenvald) have woken, remembering only a dinner and nightmares; Phillip is staying in the house. The two caretakers, Gilly Jenkin and her husband Walter Jenkin, who were away in the village overnight for supplies and a book for their ten-year-old daughter Dani, have come back up the hill and found the house changed and the party standing in the grounds. They are horrified, then relieved. They never saw or guessed what happened inside; the party may tell as much or as little as they wish.

IMPORTANT: Walter has NO spoken lines. He lost his voice and signs and writes in a worn pocket notebook. Whenever Walter "speaks", write it as a Narrator line that shows his notebook, for example: Narrator: Walter turns his notebook toward you; in a tidy hand it says: Thank the saints. Keep what he writes short and polite. The game may add one extra line itself for the case where his voice returns; do not write that.

The estate's grey cat, Wisp, is gone: the Jenkins never see him again. Gilly has noticed the cat has not been about; she is not sorry (Dani never took to him, and Dani's dog Shuck cannot abide him), but she says nothing odd about it.

VOICES:
- Gilly (speaker id gilly_jenkin): warm, quick, protective, rural West Country English. Contractions, "my lover", "my lovelies", "proper", "ent", "'tis", "bless", the odd dropped letter. Keep it readable and never a cartoon; most lines should be plain warm English with a West Country turn of phrase. She chatters, fusses, cries a little, then laughs.
- Narrator: the Vagrant, an old train conductor telling this tale afterwards in a folksy, warm, wry Southern drawl: word choice and rhythm (reckon, ain't, folks, a spell, a piece, y'all), and drop a final g ("lookin'") in about one line in three, not more. Narrator rules: second person ("you"), present tense, one or two sentences, concrete senses, no game words (no HP, roll, check, save, level, DC), never tell the player what to feel, never the word "suddenly", no facts the party could not perceive. Never mention a fiddle. Do not use {name}.

FORMAT (exactly this, nothing else): for each node, a row "~ node_id" followed by one row per line: "speaker_id [mood]: Text". Moods allowed: neutral, smile, angry, afraid, sad, sly, weary (the mood is optional; Narrator lines take none: "Narrator: Text"). Plain punctuation only: straight quotes, no em dashes, no asterisks, no markdown, no stage directions in brackets, no placeholders. A line is one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Do not write options, menus or any mechanical rows; the game's wiring is added afterwards.

NODES TO WRITE (counts are exact):

~ start   (the first meeting at the gate, morning)
 - 2 Narrator lines: the pair come up the hill road with their basket, and stop dead at the sight of the house; Gilly's hand goes to her mouth.
 - 3 lines by gilly_jenkin: horrified at how the house has changed (it looks like it has been rebuilt in the night, and wrong), then seeing the party standing safe, a flood of relief; "thank goodness you're whole".
 - 1 Narrator line: Walter's notebook, a short, shaky line of relief.

~ house   (the party says the house looks different)
 - 3 lines by gilly_jenkin: she has known that house for years; it always had a wrong note to it; this is gentler somehow, like a dog that has stopped growling, though still odd; she will get used to it.
 - 1 Narrator line: Walter's notebook, a quiet remark that he will see to the doors and the lamps.

~ couple   (the party says the Lord and Lady are safe)
 - 3 lines by gilly_jenkin: weak with relief; she was sure something was wrong; she will put the kettle on for them at once; she would not ask what the party did, and is grateful.
 - 1 Narrator line: Walter's notebook, a neat thank-you in capital letters, underlined twice.

~ dani   (asked how Dani is)
 - 3 lines by gilly_jenkin: Dani is well; she would not sleep, and said all night that the house was chewing, and Gilly told her not to be daft; now she is not so sure; she got Dani her book from town, and Dani is already halfway into it.

~ grounds   (asked whether they saw anything in the grounds)
 - 3 lines by gilly_jenkin: nothing on the road but the wind; the barn door banging; and the estate cat has not been about, she has not seen him since yesterday, and, between us, she is not sorry.

~ farewell   (the party takes its leave)
 - 2 lines by gilly_jenkin: a warm goodbye, with the offer of a hot meal whenever the party wants it.
 - 1 Narrator line: Walter's notebook, a neat goodbye.

~ again   (the party speaks to Gilly later, a short return line)
 - 2 lines by gilly_jenkin: she is busy sweeping the porch, in better spirits, and asks whether the party needs anything.

Keep the Narrator lines varied and make every Walter notebook line different in tone.
result:
~ start
Narrator: Two folks come trudgin' up the hill road lugging a heavy wicker basket between them. At the iron gate, they stop dead in their tracks.
Narrator: The woman claps both hands over her mouth as she takes in the crooked gables of the manor.
gilly_jenkin [afraid]: Merciful heavens, Walter, look at the roof and the chimneys! It looks as though the whole place were torn down in the dark and built back crooked.
gilly_jenkin [sad]: Oh, my lovelies, there you be standing on the gravel! Thank goodness you're whole, I was proper terrified for you all night.
gilly_jenkin [smile]: Bless your hearts, let me look at you. Not a soul missing, though you look worn to the bone.
Narrator: Walter fumbles his worn pocket notebook open with trembling fingers and shows you a shaky scrawl: Glad you are all still breathing.

~ house
gilly_jenkin [weary]: We've tended Druskenvald Estate for years now, and I'll tell you true, it always had a sour, wrong note to its timbers. Even on a bright morning, the halls felt like they were watching you.
gilly_jenkin [neutral]: Now it looks queer as a three-legged stool, I grant you, yet the air sits gentler somehow. 'Tis like an old dog that has finally stopped growling.
gilly_jenkin [smile]: Give me a week with a broom and some beeswax, my lover, and I'll get used to the new corners.
Narrator: Walter taps his pencil against the paper and holds up a quiet, practical note: I will check the latches and trim the lamps.

~ couple
gilly_jenkin [sad]: Oh, thank the good Lord above, my knees have gone right to water hearing that! I knew in my bones some black mischief had come down on Lord Phillip and Lady Adela.
gilly_jenkin [smile]: I'll get straight into the kitchen and put the kettle on for them at once. A hot pot of tea and fresh bread is what this morning needs.
gilly_jenkin [neutral]: I ent going to ask what you faced behind those shutters, my lovelies. Whatever you did to keep our master and mistress safe, you have our gratitude forever.
Narrator: Walter presses hard on the page and turns the notebook around, where two words sit in neat block capitals, underlined twice: THANK YOU.

~ dani
gilly_jenkin [weary]: Our little Dani is well enough, bless her, though she wouldn't shut her eyes til near dawn. Kept tugging my sleeve and swearing she could hear the big house chewing in the dark.
gilly_jenkin [afraid]: I told her not to be daft and to pull the quilt up over her ears. Looking at those twisted eaves now, I'm not so sure the child was wrong.
gilly_jenkin [smile]: Still, we fetched the storybook she wanted from the village shop, and she's already curled up by the hearth halfway through it.

~ grounds
gilly_jenkin [neutral]: There weren't nothing stirring on the lane coming up, save the autumn wind shaking the dead leaves down. Only the old barn door banging on its hinge.
gilly_jenkin [weary]: Come to think on it, I ent seen Wisp prowling the wall since yesterday morning. Usually that grey cat is under my boots begging for cream by sunrise.
gilly_jenkin [sly]: Between us, my lover, I can't say I'm sorry he's wandered off. Our Dani never took to his yellow eyes, and her dog Shuck couldn't abide the creature.

~ farewell
gilly_jenkin [smile]: Mind how you go down the hollow, my lovelies, and keep your cloaks tight against the chill. Whenever you want a hot meal and a dry chair, our kitchen door is open to you.
gilly_jenkin [neutral]: Go on with our blessing, and take care of yourselves out there.
Narrator: Walter tips his cap to y'all and holds up a fresh page penned in a steady, unhurried hand: Safe travels, friends.

~ again
gilly_jenkin [smile]: Look at the dust coming off these flagstones, my lover, a body would think nobody swept for a year! Still, with the sun out, I've got the heart for a proper tidy.
gilly_jenkin [neutral]: Do you need anything from the larder before I start on the steps, or a warm cup to hold?
